# Find a Target in Sorted Array — Explained, One Approach at a Time

<!-- Generated by scripts/gen-explained.mjs from src/data/problems/binary-search/classic-binary-search.ts.
     Edit the data, then run `npm run docs:explained`. Edits here are overwritten. -->

**Binary Search** · easy · [the same question on LeetCode](https://leetcode.com/problems/binary-search/)

Given a sorted integer array and a target, return the target's index or -1 if absent. Must run in O(log n).

## What the input promises

- 1 <= nums.length <= 10^4
- -10^4 <= nums[i], target <= 10^4
- nums is sorted ascending and every value is distinct
- return -1 when the target is absent

## Examples

| Input | Output | Why |
|---|---|---|
| `nums = [-3, 0, 4, 9, 12], target = 9` | `3` | — |
| `nums = [-3, 0, 4, 9, 12], target = 2` | `-1` | — |

<details>
<summary>Hints, one nudge at a time — open them in order</summary>

1. Compare the target with the middle element — half the array becomes irrelevant.
2. Keep an inclusive [lo, hi] range; loop while lo <= hi.
3. Off-by-one bugs live in the update: mid ± 1, never mid itself, or the loop can spin forever.

</details>

---

## 1. Linear scan

Ignore sortedness, check every element. The baseline the log bound is measured against.

```python
def binary_search(nums: list[int], target: int) -> int:
    for i, x in enumerate(nums):
        if x == target:
            return i
    return -1
```

**O(n) time · O(1) space**
<details>
<summary>The same rung in Java</summary>

```java
public int binarySearch(int[] nums, int target) {
    for (int i = 0; i < nums.length; i++) {
        if (nums[i] == target) return i;
    }
    return -1;
}
```

</details>
<details>
<summary>The same rung in C++</summary>

```cpp
int binarySearch(const vector<int>& nums, int target) {
    for (int i = 0; i < (int)nums.size(); i++) {
        if (nums[i] == target) return i;
    }
    return -1;
}
```

</details>

## 2. Recursive

> **Why now.** Checking every element ignores the only thing the input promises: order. Halving the range uses it, and the halving reads most naturally as a recursion.

Same halving, expressed recursively. Cleaner to some eyes, costs stack frames; iterative is the production default.

```python
def binary_search(nums: list[int], target: int) -> int:
    def go(lo: int, hi: int) -> int:
        if lo > hi:
            return -1
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2
        if nums[mid] == target:
            return mid
        if nums[mid] < target:
            return go(mid + 1, hi)
        return go(lo, mid - 1)

    return go(0, len(nums) - 1)
```

**O(log n) time · O(log n) stack space**
<details>
<summary>The same rung in Java</summary>

```java
public int binarySearch(int[] nums, int target) {
    return binarySearch(nums, target, 0, nums.length - 1);
}
private int binarySearch(int[] nums, int target, int lo, int hi) {
    if (lo > hi) return -1;
    int mid = (lo + hi) / 2;
    if (nums[mid] == target) return mid;
    if (nums[mid] < target) return binarySearch(nums, target, mid + 1, hi);
    return binarySearch(nums, target, lo, mid - 1);
}
```

</details>
<details>
<summary>The same rung in C++</summary>

```cpp
int binarySearchHelper(const vector<int>& nums, int target, int lo, int hi) {
    if (lo > hi) return -1;
    int mid = (lo + hi) / 2;
    if (nums[mid] == target) return mid;
    if (nums[mid] < target) return binarySearchHelper(nums, target, mid + 1, hi);
    return binarySearchHelper(nums, target, lo, mid - 1);
}

int binarySearch(const vector<int>& nums, int target) {
    return binarySearchHelper(nums, target, 0, (int)nums.size() - 1);
}
```

</details>

## 3. The one to remember

> **Why now.** Recursion pays a stack frame per halving and buys nothing. The same loop written iteratively is constant space, and it is the version to write under pressure.

Maintain an inclusive search range [lo, hi] that must contain the target if it exists. Probe the midpoint: equal means done; smaller means the answer lives strictly right of mid; larger means strictly left. Each probe halves the range, giving the logarithmic bound.

```python
def binary_search(nums: list[int], target: int) -> int:
    lo, hi = 0, len(nums) - 1
    while lo <= hi:
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2
        if nums[mid] == target:
            return mid
        if nums[mid] < target:
            lo = mid + 1
        else:
            hi = mid - 1
    return -1
```

**O(log n) time · O(1) space**
<details>
<summary>The same rung in Java</summary>

```java
public int binarySearch(int[] nums, int target) {
    int lo = 0, hi = nums.length - 1;
    while (lo <= hi) {
        int mid = (lo + hi) / 2;
        if (nums[mid] == target) return mid;
        if (nums[mid] < target) lo = mid + 1;
        else hi = mid - 1;
    }
    return -1;
}
```

</details>
<details>
<summary>The same rung in C++</summary>

```cpp
int binarySearch(const vector<int>& nums, int target) {
    int lo = 0, hi = (int)nums.size() - 1;
    while (lo <= hi) {
        int mid = (lo + hi) / 2;
        if (nums[mid] == target) return mid;
        if (nums[mid] < target) lo = mid + 1;
        else hi = mid - 1;
    }
    return -1;
}
```

</details>

## The arc

| # | Approach | Cost | What it adds |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Linear scan | O(n) time · O(1) space | the baseline — nothing before it |
| 2 | Recursive | O(log n) time · O(log n) stack space | Checking every element ignores the only thing the input promises: order. Halving the range uses it, and the halving reads most naturally as a recursion. |
| 3 | The one to remember | O(log n) time · O(1) space | Recursion pays a stack frame per halving and buys nothing. The same loop written iteratively is constant space, and it is the version to write under pressure. |

## Full runnable script

Every rung in one file, printed against the inputs `npm run verify:run`
drives the Java and C++ blocks with. Run it: `python explained.py`.

```python
def binary_search_linear_scan(nums: list[int], target: int) -> int:
    for i, x in enumerate(nums):
        if x == target:
            return i
    return -1


def binary_search_recursive(nums: list[int], target: int) -> int:
    def go(lo: int, hi: int) -> int:
        if lo > hi:
            return -1
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2
        if nums[mid] == target:
            return mid
        if nums[mid] < target:
            return go(mid + 1, hi)
        return go(lo, mid - 1)

    return go(0, len(nums) - 1)


def binary_search_the_one_to_remember(nums: list[int], target: int) -> int:
    lo, hi = 0, len(nums) - 1
    while lo <= hi:
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2
        if nums[mid] == target:
            return mid
        if nums[mid] < target:
            lo = mid + 1
        else:
            hi = mid - 1
    return -1

APPROACHES = [
    binary_search_linear_scan,
    binary_search_recursive,
    binary_search_the_one_to_remember,
]

# the same inputs npm run verify:run drives the Java and C++ blocks with:
# a target past both ends of the array — [[3],5] would read off the end if hi started at n
CASES = [
    lambda: ([3], 5),
    lambda: ([-1,0,3,5,9,12], 9),
    lambda: ([-1,0,3,5,9,12], 2),
    lambda: ([5], 5),
    lambda: ([5], -5),
]

if __name__ == "__main__":
    for fn in APPROACHES:
        answers = []
        for make in CASES:
            try:
                answers.append(fn(*make()))
            except BaseException as exc:  # a rung that raises names itself
                answers.append(f"!{exc}")
        print(f"{fn.__name__:<35} -> {answers}")
```
